1:
A new reign opens in Jerusalem, and the witnesses treat the bare accession-notice as the doorway into a chapter of divided character — a king who begins well and ends an apostate. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays the whole arc out in advance: Amaziah succeeds his father Joash and begins his reign well; he executes his father's murderers but spares their children; he reviews and remodels the army and hires a hundred thousand soldiers out of Israel, only to send them home again at a prophet's word; he attacks the Edomites, kills ten thousand and hurls ten thousand more from a rock; the dismissed Israelites ravage the cities of Judah; and then, fatally, the conqueror turns idolater, is reproved by a prophet whom he threatens into silence, challenges Joash of Israel, is overthrown and taken prisoner, and at last dies in a conspiracy at Lachish. Twenty-nine years are compressed into a single line, and all of this lies folded within it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the reign as the tragedy of half-heartedness. Amaziah, he says, did that which was right in the eyes of the LORD — he worshipped the true God, kept the temple service going, and countenanced religion in his kingdom — yet he did it not with a perfect heart; he was no enemy to religion, but a cool and indifferent friend, and such, Henry adds, is the character of too many in a Laodicean age, who do that which is good, but not with the whole heart. It is a portrait, not yet of wickedness, but of a piety without fire; and Henry, who knows how such a temper ends, sets it at the head of the chapter as a warning.

The accession facts themselves the witnesses let stand in their plainness: Amaziah came to the throne at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years, his mother Jehoaddan a woman of Jerusalem, so that on both sides he was rooted in the city of David. The length of the reign is deceptive, for its strength lay at the front and its ruin at the close. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke maps the road the chapter will travel; Henry names the flaw that will send the king down it. Between them they frame a life poised between a good beginning and a bad end, and they leave the reader to watch how a heart not wholly given to God is slowly claimed by everything else.
2:
The chronicler's opening verdict on Amaziah is a divided one, and the witnesses fasten on the qualifying clause that shadows the praise. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the sentence at face value — he did what was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not with a perfect heart — and read it as the key to all that follows, in which an outward conformity to true religion proves too shallow to hold when victory and pride arrive. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the trajectory: Amaziah began his reign well, but soon became an idolater, as the darker turn at v.14 will show; the good beginning was no guarantee of a good end.

John Wesley, of the same school, presses the phrase into a diagnosis of the man's whole religion. He was not an enemy to religion, Wesley says, but a cool and indifferent friend; not a man of serious piety, for his heart was not whole with God. The half-heartedness is no minor blemish but the very fault-line along which the reign will crack — a devotion correct in its forms and hollow at its centre. It is the piety of a man who honours God with the establishment of the kingdom while withholding the heart, and Wesley refuses to flatter it into anything more than it was.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers all this into his memorable verdict. Amaziah worshipped the true God, kept the temple service going, and countenanced religion in his kingdom, so that he was no enemy to it; but he had no zeal for its exercises and no serious devotion of his own. Such, Henry laments, is the character of too many in a Laodicean age: they do that which is good, but not with the heart, not with a perfect heart. It is the religion of a man who will keep the true worship so long as it costs him nothing, and forsake it the moment a rival attraction offers.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil fixes the verdict as the reign's interpretive key; Clarke marks the descent from a fair beginning to idolatry; Wesley and Henry expose the coolness of heart beneath the fair exterior. Between them they show why the chronicler will not simply call Amaziah good: a heart divided is a heart already half-lost, and the same king who kept the temple service going will presently bow to the gods of Seir. The praise and the warning stand together in one sentence, and the chapter is the unfolding of both.
3:
With the throne secured, Amaziah's first recorded act is an execution, and the witnesses read it as rough justice held within the bounds of law. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the opening clause — "the kingdom was established to him," or better, the sovereignty was confirmed to him — marking the moment the young king felt strong enough to move. His fellow witness Keil and Delitzsch set the deed in sequence: as soon as the kingdom was established, Amaziah slew the servants who had killed the king his father, the courtiers who had conspired against Joash and struck him down in the previous reign. That the king waited until his power was secure is itself a mark of prudence; he did not risk his throne to avenge his father before the throne was safe.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the morality with characteristic honesty. It was, he grants, a necessary piece of justice that Amaziah put the traitors to death; and he raises the hard question squarely. Though we may suppose the murderers meant to avenge upon their king the blood of the prophet Zechariah, slain at Joash's order in 2 Chronicles 24:21, this could by no means justify their wickedness, for they were not the appointed avengers but presumptuously took God's work out of his own hands. Amaziah therefore did what became him in calling them to account, and the deed stands to his credit as a real, if grim, act of justice. Henry is careful not to let the murderers' possible motive excuse their crime: a wrong done to a prophet is no warrant for a subject to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, and the king who avenged his father was, in this, the arm of the law and not of private grudge.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, in his survey of the chapter, notes the same double movement that the next verse will complete: the king slays his father's murderers but spares their children. The pairing is deliberate, for the restraint of v.4 is what keeps this execution from becoming a dynastic massacre.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the timing in the words "established to him"; Keil fixes the identity of the slain; Henry defends the justice while refusing to whitewash the assassins; Clarke sets the deed beside the mercy that limits it. Between them they show a king beginning his reign as he ought — punishing treason, honouring his murdered father, and yet, as the next verse will make plain, submitting even his vengeance to the written law of God. It is the best of Amaziah, done while his heart was still, in its cool way, right with the LORD.
4:
Where a lesser king would have extirpated the whole families of the conspirators, Amaziah stopped at the guilty — "he slew not their children" — and the witnesses honour the restraint and trace it to the law. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the king acted expressly "as it is written in the law in the book of Moses," where the LORD commanded that the fathers shall not die for the children, neither the children for the fathers, but every man shall die for his own sin. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, fixes the references precisely: the verse coincides almost exactly with the parallel at 2 Kings 14:6, and the statute invoked is Deuteronomy 24:16, which the older account in Kings reproduces even more exactly than the chronicler does here. Ellicott marks the small grammatical shift too — where Kings has "every man shall die for his own sin" in the singular, the chronicler writes it in the plural, "each in his own sin shall they be put to death."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke both single out this clemency in their surveys of the reign. Henry observes that Amaziah forbade the putting of the children to death for their parents' sin; Clarke, that he spares their children. In an age when the fall of a house commonly meant the sword for every male in it, the young king's deliberate self-limitation is remarkable, and the witnesses will not let it pass unpraised. That the chronicler and the older writer alike pause to quote the statute in full shows how notable the restraint appeared to those who recorded it — a king reaching for the book of Moses to govern the very moment when a lesser man would have let his anger run.

What gives the restraint its weight is the principle behind it: individual responsibility before God. The children of traitors are not chargeable with their fathers' treason; every soul shall answer for its own sin and no other. That Amaziah reached for the book of Moses to govern even his vengeance shows a conscience still tutored by the law, and it stands in bright contrast to the ruthlessness he will show the Edomite prisoners at v.12, where no such mercy restrains his hand.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the law and the parallel; Henry and Clarke honour the mercy. Between them they show a king who, at his best, bent his own power to the written word of God — sparing the innocent because Scripture forbade their blood, and so keeping his justice clean of the tyrant's usual excess.
5:
Turning from justice to war, Amaziah numbers his fighting men, and the witnesses read the muster both as sound generalship and as a silent index of Judah's decline. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the process: the king assembled Judah, ordered them by the captains of thousands and of hundreds throughout all Judah and Benjamin, and took a census of all liable to military service from twenty years old and upward, finding three hundred thousand choice men able to bear the spear and target. It is, they observe, a relatively small number — small not only beside the manifestly swollen figures of Jehoshaphat at 2 Chronicles 17:14, but beside the earlier muster of Asa; and they account for the shrinkage by the disastrous wars of Joram at 2 Chronicles 21:17, the losses under Ahaziah, and above all the defeat Joash had lately suffered from the Syrians at 2 Chronicles 24:23.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, confirms every point and adds the philologist's touches: the men were marshalled "according to father houses," mustered from twenty years old, the military age set at Numbers 1:2; the phrase "able to go forth to war" is literally "going out in the host," and "that could handle spear and shield" denotes the heavy-armed warrior. The three hundred thousand, he grants, is immensely below the forces of Jehoshaphat and little more than half of Asa's; all such high numbers are open to suspicion, yet a certain relative propriety marks this one, for the kingdom had truly suffered great losses in the reigns just past.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supply the motive. Gill notes simply that the king gathered the inhabitants of Judah; Clarke explains that Amaziah purposed to avenge himself upon the Edomites and wished first to know his military strength before coming to a rupture. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral the bare figure implies: in Jehoshaphat's time, fifty or sixty years before, the men fit for war were four times as many, and this decline is no accident. Sin, Henry says, weakens a people, diminishes them, dispirits them, and lessens their number and their figure; the shrunken muster is the visible cost of a generation's apostasy.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the census and its diminished total; Gill and Clarke name the coming Edomite war; Henry reads in the small number the weakening hand of judgment. Between them they show a king counting a reduced army — enough, as the next verses will insist, only if the LORD be with it.
6:
Judging his own diminished army too weak, Amaziah reaches across the border and buys an alliance — "he hired an hundred thousand mighty men of valour out of Israel for an hundred talents of silver" — and the witnesses read the transaction as the first misstep of the campaign. The reformed John Gill states the reason plainly: judging his own force insufficient for the expedition he was meditating against the Edomites, the king took into his pay a hundred thousand men from the ten tribes. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the hiring at the head of the prophetic episode that follows, for it is precisely this mercenary corps that the man of God will command him to send home.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, weighs the numbers and the money. The figure, he suspects, has suffered in transmission, though the critic Thenius pronounces the hiring itself historical even though the older record in Kings does not mention it; the hundred talents of silver he reckons at something near forty thousand pounds of his own currency, while frankly admitting that what such a sum represented in Amaziah's day cannot be determined with certainty. What is certain is the policy: a king short of soldiers thought to make up the deficiency with his treasury.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the fault in that policy. Finding his own kingdom deficient in men, Amaziah thought to supply the want with his money and took into his pay a hundred thousand Israelites. Had he consulted any of his prophets first, Henry says, or but considered how little any of his ancestors had gained by their alliances with the northern kingdom, he would not have had this to undo again; but rashness makes work for repentance. The hiring looks prudent — more men for the fight — yet it rests on a distrust of God and a partnership with an apostate people, and both faults will have to be repented before the campaign can go forward.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the motive; Ellicott weighs the suspect number and the price; Keil sets the hiring as the occasion of the prophet's word; Henry exposes the rashness underneath. Between them they show a king solving a shortage of faith with a surplus of silver — buying the swords of men from whom, as the next verse will declare, the LORD had departed. It is a bargain that will cost him a hundred talents and teach him that the strength of Judah was never a matter of numbers.
7:
A prophet intercepts the campaign before it starts — "let not the army of Israel go with thee" — and the witnesses gather around both the messenger and his reason. The reformed John Gill notes only the man's anonymity, recording and dismissing the rabbinic guess that this unnamed man of God was Amos, the father of Isaiah, a fancy he says rests on no foundation. What matters is not his name but his word: the hired Israelites must be sent home.

The ground of the command is a single sentence — "the LORD is not with Israel." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains the added gloss, "to wit, with all the children of Ephraim," as the chronicler's own definition of the term Israel, Ephraim being the standing name of the northern kingdom in the prophets, as in Hosea 5:11; and he sets the prophet's principle beside the like rebukes of ungodly alliances at 2 Chronicles 19:2 and 2 Chronicles 16:7. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds the Targum's paraphrase, that the Word of the LORD is not the helper of the Israelites nor of the kingdom of the tribe of Ephraim — the calf-worshippers from whom God had withdrawn.

John Wesley, of the same school, draws the practical lesson. It is comfortable, he says, to employ those who, we have reason to hope, have an interest in heaven, but dangerous to associate with those from whom the Lord is departed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the point into strategy: God had no delight in the children of Ephraim, because they were not with him but worshipped the calves, and this was reason enough not to use them, for what good could be expected from men who had not God with them, nor his blessing upon their undertakings? To lean on such allies was to lean on a broken reed.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill clears away the false name; Ellicott and Clarke fix the meaning of "Israel" and "Ephraim" and the withdrawn favour of God; Wesley and Henry draw the abiding caution against yoking oneself to the godless. Between them they show that the prophet's objection was not military but spiritual: the hundred thousand were strong men, but the strength that decides battles is the presence of the LORD, and that presence had forsaken the calf-kingdom. Amaziah is bidden to choose between a hired army and a present God — and the next verses will test whether he can.
8:
The prophet's next words are among the hardest in the chapter, and the witnesses divide over how to read them — "but if thou wilt go, do it, be strong for the battle: God shall make thee fall before the enemy." Taken as they stand, the sentence seems to promise defeat to the very man it urges to courage, and the schools resolve the paradox in opposite ways.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley read it as irony. Gill calls "if thou wilt go, do it, be strong for the battle" an ironical expression: if thou wilt not be advised, take the Israelites with thee, exert all thy courage and skill, and mark the issue. Wesley agrees that "do it" is an ironical concession, like the prophet's "go, and prosper" elsewhere — a dare, not a blessing, whose true sense is that with such allies the king will surely fall.

The grammatical-historical witnesses find rather a wound in the text. Charles Ellicott judges that before the words "God shall make thee fall" the Hebrew for "and not" must have dropped out, so that the prophet's real meaning is, "Venture on the expedition by thyself, with a good courage, and God will not let thee stumble before the foe"; and he notes candidly that no ancient version inserts the required negative, so the omission is very old, the LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac all struggling with the passage. Keil and Delitzsch reason to the same sense from the other side: the undoubted thought of the verse is that Amaziah is to go alone, show himself valiant, and be helped by the LORD to conquer — a thought the traditional Masoretic text does not seem to contain, which is why Clericus was driven to take the words ironically. The clause that closes the verse both schools read alike: "for God hath power to help, and to cast down" — the LORD can give victory with a small band or defeat with a great one, so that numbers decide nothing.

So the debate is real, though the practical upshot is one. Gill and Wesley keep the received text and make it bitter irony; Ellicott and Keil restore a lost negative and make it a straight promise to the king who will trust God rather than mercenaries. Either way the message to Amaziah is identical: dismiss the men of Israel, go in the strength of the LORD, and the God who holds both help and ruin in his hand will not fail thee. The witnesses contend only over the grammar of the warning, not over its force.
9:
The king's first thought is not of obedience but of his money — "what shall we do for the hundred talents which I have given to the army of Israel?" — and the witnesses read both the anxiety and the answer that quiets it. The reformed John Gill hears the note of reluctance: Amaziah spoke with some concern, as one loath to lose so large a sum, feeling that the advance already paid to the Israelites could not be demanded back. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the exchange: the king, minded to heed the prophet, asked only what he should do about the hundred talents paid to the mercenaries, and the man of God answered that Jahve could give him far more than that. Thereupon, they add, he dismissed the hired Ephraimites — the verb meaning that he separated them off from his army made ready for battle, that they might return to their place. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, glosses the king's blunt Hebrew — "what to do?", that is, what must we do? — and identifies "the army" as the troop of mercenaries, the hired band.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a lesson on the economics of obedience. This, he says, is the objection men often raise against their duty — they are afraid of losing by it. But the prophet's reply sweeps the fear away: the LORD is able to give thee much more than this. What are a hundred talents between the king and his God? He has ways enough to make up the loss; it is below a king to speak of it. A firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to bear us out in our duty, Henry urges, and to make up all the loss and damage we sustain in his service, will make his yoke easy and his burden light. And Henry notes the sequel that proved the promise: this very sum, a hundred talents, was afterward given as tribute to Amaziah's grandson Jotham at 2 Chronicles 27:5, so that the principal was repaid, and with it interest of wheat and barley beside.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill catches the reluctance; Keil and Ellicott fix the dismissal and the terms; Henry draws the abiding lesson of trust. Between them they show the true cost of the alliance — not a hundred talents, but the temptation to weigh silver against the word of God. Amaziah asks the question every reluctant conscience asks, "but what shall we do for the money?", and receives the only answer that matters: the God who commands the sacrifice is able to repay it a hundredfold.
10:
Amaziah obeys, and the obedience costs him at once — he sends the hired Israelites home, and they depart in a fury that will presently turn to bloodshed. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the king separated them from his army, among whom they had been incorporated and ranked. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the same act and its consequence: he separated the host that had come to him out of Ephraim, to go home again, whereupon their anger was greatly kindled against Judah and they returned in great heat. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, renders the phrase "home in great anger" as departing to their own place in a heat of anger, and reads the cause without difficulty: the dismissed force would be incensed at treatment that seemed to brand them untrustworthy and that robbed them of the plunder a victorious campaign would have brought.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses agree on the motive. Adam Clarke says they thought themselves insulted and began to meditate revenge, referring the reader to the fuller treatment of these events at 2 Kings 14:1 and following. John Wesley reckons the double grievance exactly: their anger was kindled because they were both disgraced by the rejection and disappointed of the spoil they had hoped to gain, being sent away empty — for the hundred talents, he supposes, had gone only to their officers to raise the men, not into the common soldier's hand.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the whole transaction to the king's honour. Amaziah would rather lose his money, disoblige his allies, and dismiss a fourth part of his army just as they were about to take the field, than offend God; and this obedience, Henry says, is upon record to his credit. Yet he understands the offence given: the Israelites went home in great anger, taking it as an affront to be made fools of and cashiered as men not fit to be employed, disappointed of the profit and reputation they had promised themselves. Men are apt, Henry observes, to resent whatever touches them in their profit or their pride, even when it frees them from trouble.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the separation; Ellicott, Clarke, and Wesley expose the double grievance of disgrace and lost booty; Henry sets the king's costly obedience against the mercenaries' wounded pride. Between them they show the price of doing right — a fourth of the army gone, an ally offended, and a smouldering resentment that will soon fall upon the defenceless towns of Judah. Obedience, the chapter quietly warns, is not always followed by ease; sometimes it is followed by the anger of the men one has done right to dismiss.
11:
Freed of his hired allies, Amaziah goes to war on the strength of the prophet's word, and the witnesses mark the courage the moment required. The reformed John Gill notes that the king was not discouraged by the dismission of the hired troops but, trusting in the promise and power of God, led forth his people with boldness and intrepidity to fight the Edomites. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the key verb — "Amaziah strengthened himself" means he showed himself strong, took courage, exactly as the prophet had bidden him do at v.8 — and locates the battlefield: the Valley of Salt, lying to the south-east of the Dead Sea, the same ground named in David's day at 2 Samuel 8:13. There he smote ten thousand of the children of Seir.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, tie the courage tightly to the command that authorised it: the verb "strengthened himself" reaches back to the prophet's "be strong for the battle," so that Amaziah's boldness is not bravado but obedience — he showed himself strong according to the word of God, and led his people into the Valley of Salt, where the ten thousand fell. And Ellicott sets the victory beside the parallel notice in Kings, where the same triumph is recorded with the added detail that the king took the Edomite stronghold of Sela and renamed it Joktheel, at 2 Kings 14:7.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying the campaign, marks the scale of the slaughter: the king left ten thousand dead upon the spot, in the very field of battle, before the grimmer sequel of the prisoners. The point on which the witnesses converge is the vindication of faith: the army Amaziah had feared too small, once purged of the men from whom God had departed, proved more than enough, because the LORD was now with it. The reduced host of Judah, marching in obedience, did what the swollen host could never have done in disobedience.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill reads the boldness of a king trusting God; Ellicott and Keil fix the verb, the valley, and the fallen ten thousand, and tie the courage to the prophet's charge; Henry counts the dead. Between them they show the promise of v.8 made good — that God had power to help without the hired thousands — and a king, for this one bright hour, strong in the strength the LORD supplied. The tragedy is that the same hand which now wins so signal a victory will, in the next verse, stain it with needless cruelty, and in the verses after, throw its Giver away.
12:
The victory turns to atrocity — ten thousand more Edomites taken alive are carried to a cliff-top and flung down — and the witnesses neither excuse the deed nor let it go unexamined. The reformed John Gill records the fact that the rest of the Edomite army, an equal number, fell into the hands of Judah and were carried off captive. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the end of those captives without flinching: the children of Judah brought them to the top of the rock and cast them down, so that they were all broken in pieces.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, translates carefully — "and ten thousand the sons of Judah took alive" — and glosses "the top of the rock" as the head of Sela, the Edomite capital known to later ages as Petra, "the crag," perhaps the name of a cliff overhanging the town. The savage massacre of the prisoners, he grants, is not mentioned in Kings, but it is entirely credible in view of the well-known atrocities of ancient warfare, and he sets it among a row of grim parallels — the treatment of captives at 1 Chronicles 20:3, the bitter cry of Psalms 137:9, the cruelties denounced in Amos 1:11, and Joab's slaughter of every male in Edom at 1 Kings 11:15. He finds it remarkable, though, that the chronicler nowhere mentions the capture of Sela itself, which the older record does; and here a genuine question opens.

For the critic Thenius, whom Ellicott reports, supposed that this whole verse is really a corrupt attempt to restore an illegible text of the parallel at 2 Kings 14:7 — that the massacre of prisoners is a scribe's misreading of the taking of Sela. Ellicott and Keil reject this: the detail is credible independent information, not a botched copy, and the chronicler often preserves what Kings omits. So the debate is drawn between a genuine tradition and a garbled restoration.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry passes the severest moral judgment. The king killed all ten thousand by throwing them down some steep and craggy precipice; what provocation he had to this cruelty we are not told, but it was certainly very severe — a needless barbarity fastened upon a victory already won. The witnesses do not divide over the horror, only over the text: Gill and Keil fix the deed, Ellicott sets it among the cruelties of the age and defends its historicity against Thenius, and Henry names it for the savagery it was. Between them they show the shadow that falls across Amaziah's triumph — the same hand that spared the children of traitors now hurls ten thousand helpless prisoners to their deaths.
13:
The dismissed Israelites take their revenge while Amaziah is away winning his war — "the soldiers of the army which Amaziah sent back fell on the cities of Judah" — and the witnesses trace both the raid and the providence behind it. The reformed John Gill identifies the raiders as the hundred thousand hired out of Israel, whom the king had dismissed before marching against Edom. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the foray: the Ephraimite host fell plundering upon the cities of Judah from Samaria even to Beth-horon, smote three thousand of the inhabitants, and carried away great spoil. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, sharpens the verb — they "fell upon," that is attacked with intent to plunder, as at Job 1:17 — and locates Beth-horon by its earlier notice at 1 Chronicles 7:24.

Over the words "from Samaria" a genuine difficulty opens, and the two grammatical-historical witnesses weigh it. The natural reading is that the mercenaries wasted these towns on their way home; but "from Samaria to Beth-horon" seems to name Samaria as the starting-point of the raid, not its limit — which would mean the men first returned home and then set out afresh from the northern capital. Ellicott suspects the word "Samaria" is corrupt; Keil records the alternative, that the attack was carried out only later, from Samaria as its base. So the debate stands between a raid made on the homeward march and a second, deliberate incursion mounted from the north.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lifts the whole episode into providence. Why should God suffer this, when the men were sent home in obedience to his own word? Because, Wesley answers, God thus chastised those cities of Judah for their idolatries, which were found most in the parts that lay next to Israel; the men of Israel had corrupted them, and now the same men were made a plague to them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it exactly so: God's way is in the sea, and the very allies dismissed by his command are permitted to scourge the border towns whose idolatry had been caught from them — Satan, as Henry says, both tempts and torments, first seducing men to sin and then afflicting them for it.

The witnesses do not divide over the meaning, only over the route. Gill names the raiders; Keil and Ellicott fix the plunder and dispute the geography; Wesley and Henry read the raid as God's chastisement of Judah's border idolatry by the hand of its own corrupters. Between them they show that even a righteous obedience may be overruled to a further end: Amaziah did right to send the mercenaries home, and God used their resentment to punish sins the king's campaign had not touched.
14:
The chapter's hinge is a stunning apostasy — Amaziah comes home from smiting the Edomites and brings their gods with him — and the witnesses labour over both the folly of the act and the puzzle of its record. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch state the deed plainly: on his return from the war in which he had smitten the Edomites, the king brought the images of the gods of the children of Seir, set them up as his own gods, bowed himself before them, and burned incense to them. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, illumines the custom of carrying off a conquered people's idols from the Assyrian inscriptions, which repeatedly record such captures; he fixes "the children of Seir" as the tribal name of the Edomites at 1 Chronicles 1:38, and reads the closing verbs as describing a settled, habitual practice — before them he would bow, to them he would offer incense.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the sheer absurdity of it. Egregious folly! To worship the gods of the nation he had just conquered — gods that could not protect their own worshippers from his sword — was the greatest absurdity imaginable; there was more colour, Henry says, in Ahaz's later worship of the gods of those who had conquered him at 2 Chronicles 28:23, but none at all here. Had Amaziah cast these idols down from the rock and broken them to pieces, as he had the prisoners, he would have shown more of the piety and the pity of an Israelite; perhaps, Henry suggests, for that barbarous inhumanity he was now given up to this ridiculous idolatry. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds only the Targum's identification of the gods as the idols of the children of Gebal.

But a real question hangs over the verse, for the older account at 2 Kings 14 says the king did what was right. Ellicott meets it directly: the chronicler portrays Amaziah in a darker light, which proves not contradiction but independence of judgment and the possession of additional information; the setting up of these gods need not mean he abandoned the worship of Jehovah, any more than Ahaz did. The critic Thenius held that the notice contradicts Kings, and Thenius and Bertheau supposed the chronicler merely inferred the idolatry from the king's later ill success; Ellicott answers that it was more likely drawn from one of the histories he used. So the debate is whether Amaziah's idol-worship is genuine tradition or theological inference. The witnesses do not divide over the folly, only over the source: Keil and Ellicott affirm the fact and the Assyrian custom behind it; Henry marvels at the madness of it; Clarke names the gods. Between them they show a conqueror kneeling to the defeated — and mark the exact point where a divided heart tips over into ruin.
15:
Heaven answers the apostasy with a prophet and a devastating question. The reformed John Gill marks why the anger of the LORD was kindled against Amaziah: idolatry is always highly displeasing to God, and this was a peculiarly provoking instance, for when the LORD had given him victory over his enemies he turned and worshipped the very gods of the vanquished. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch report the sending and the message: God, in his anger, sent a prophet who asked, "Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?" The logic is unanswerable — gods that could not save their worshippers from Amaziah's sword are no gods to save Amaziah.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, renders the taunt more sharply — the gods "delivered not" their people — and sets it beside the like boast of Sennacherib over the impotent gods of the nations at 2 Kings 18:33. He adds the historian's illumination, gathering from Assyrian and Edomite names the very deities Amaziah may have courted: Hadad, and Kôsh, whose name stands in the royal names of Edom, and even Moloch, whose worship a king's name attests among them. The king's object, Ellicott suggests, may have been to win the favour of these local powers and so keep his hold on the territory he had conquered — a piece of religious statecraft as faithless as it was futile.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the abiding lesson from the prophet's question. Before God sent to destroy Amaziah, he sent to convince and reclaim him; the prophet reasoned with him fairly and mildly — why seek the favour of gods that could not deliver their own people? If men would but duly consider the inability of all those things to which they have recourse when they forsake God, Henry says, they would not be such enemies to themselves. The whole force of the reproof lies in that exposed absurdity.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the provocation; Keil and Ellicott fix the prophet's question and the powerless gods it mocks; Henry reads it as mercy before judgment, reason before ruin. Between them they show the patience of God with a straying king: the same LORD whose anger is justly kindled sends first not a sword but a syllogism, laying bare the folly of trusting powers he had himself just proven helpless. The tragedy of the next verse is that Amaziah, faced with a question he cannot answer, chooses to silence the questioner instead.
16:
Confronted, Amaziah does not repent but threatens, and the witnesses read the silencing of the prophet as the moment the king seals his own doom. The reformed John Gill fastens on the king's retort — "Art thou made of the king's counsel?" — and answers it: the prophet was not indeed one of Amaziah's privy council, but he was appointed a counsellor by the Lord, the King of kings, to expostulate with him about his idolatry, and to that counsel the king was bound to hearken. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the sting of the Hebrew — "a counsellor to the king have we appointed thee?" — and hears the prophet turn the king's own word back on him: when the man of God says "God hath counselled to destroy thee," he is appropriating the very term Amaziah had flung at him, claiming a place in the divine council the king had denied him in the royal one. Keil and Delitzsch read the collective "we appointed thee" as the royal plural, the king speaking for himself and his court, and note that the prophet ceased at the threat, answering only that he knew God had determined to destroy the king because he had done this and would not hearken.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the psychology of the secure sinner. "Who art thou," the king means, "that presumest to direct my affairs without my commission?" The secure sinner, Wesley observes, values himself on having silenced his reprovers and monitors; but what comes of it? It is a plain indication that he is marked out for ruin, for those who are deaf to reproof are ripening apace for destruction.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays bare the whole ugly scene. The king could say nothing to excuse his folly, so he fell into a passion with the reprover — taunting him as meddling in what was above him, silencing him with "forbear," and threatening him with the fate of the prophet Zechariah in the last reign, so that he made himself guilty of that earlier blood as well. And Henry marks the terrible contrast: Amaziah had readily obeyed the prophet who bade him dismiss the army, though it cost him a hundred talents, but ran upon this one with an unaccountable rage — willing to part with his talents of silver, but by no means with his gods of silver. The witchcraft of idolatry, Henry says, had bewitched him; and the doom the prophet pronounces is that of Ephraim, "joined to idols; let him alone," at Hosea 4:17.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the king's word and the prophet's turning of it; Keil marks the ceasing; Wesley and Henry read the silencing as the seal of ruin. Between them they show a man who would rather lose a heavenly monitor than a worthless idol — and so is left alone with it.
17:
Flushed with his Edomite victory and deaf to the prophet, Amaziah now provokes a stronger king, and the witnesses read the challenge as pride hurrying to its fall. The reformed John Gill notes the fatal quality of the counsel behind it: Amaziah "took advice," but not of God nor of his prophets, only of some of his nobles as vain as himself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch report the challenge to Joash king of Israel — "Come, let us see one another in the face" — and observe that instead of following the prophet's warning the king consulted his courtiers and defied his neighbour; the war that followed, so fatal to Amaziah and to Judah, is told also in the older record at 2 Kings 14:8. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, glosses "took advice" as took counsel, the counsel opposite to what the prophet would have given at v.16, and renders the challenge literally — "let us look one another in the face," as combatants do.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a study in the ruin of pride. Never was a proud prince more thoroughly mortified; and the whole disaster verifies two of Solomon's proverbs — that a man's pride shall bring him low, at Proverbs 29:23, and that he who goes forth hastily to strive will not know what to do in the end thereof, when his neighbour has put him to shame, at Proverbs 25:8. Henry marks what is new here beyond the parallel in Kings: Amaziah took advice, but of statesmen who would flatter him and bid him go up and prosper, not of the prophet, who was not made of the king's counsel. It is good to take advice, Henry allows, but of those fit to advise us; and those who will not take counsel from the word of God, which would guide them aright, are justly left to the bad advice of men who counsel them to their destruction.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in fewer words: the king took advice about the injury the Israelite raiders had done his people and how to repair it, but took it with his flattering statesmen and not with the prophet — good to take advice, but of them who are fit to advise.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley name the flattering counsellors; Keil and Ellicott fix the challenge and its parallel; Henry reads the pride that Solomon's proverbs foredoom. Between them they show a king intoxicated by one victory rushing to a second war — and choosing, at the crisis, the counsel that would gratify his pride over the word that would have saved his throne.
18:
Joash answers the challenge not with defiance but with a fable, and the witnesses unfold the parable's cutting scorn. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch relate it in full: the thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, "Give thy daughter to my son to wife"; and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon and trode down the thistle. The little weed presumes to treat as an equal with the great tree, and is crushed by a passing brute for its pains — a picture, aimed straight at Amaziah, of a small king puffed up to challenge a greater and about to be trampled for his presumption.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers the reader to the fuller exposition of the same fable in the parallel at 2 Kings 14:9, and adds the Targum's pointed application, which turns the parable into direct reproach: thus hast thou done, it says, when thou didst send and lead up from Israel a hundred thousand warriors for a hundred talents of silver, and then, after they were sent, wouldst not let them go with thee to war but sent them back enraged, so that they spread over the country, cut off three thousand, and carried back much spoil. The Targum thus binds Joash's taunt to the very grievance of the dismissed mercenaries at v.13.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole exchange as the meeting of two faults. Amaziah's challenge was foolish, and Joash's answer haughty and scornful; yet folded within that scorn was friendly advice — a warning to sit still and know when he was well off. The thistle-and-cedar fable was contemptuous, but it was also true, and had Amaziah heeded the mockery he might have kept his crown. The tragedy is that a proud man will bear anything sooner than the humbling counsel of an enemy who happens to be right.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil relates the fable; Clarke ties it, through the Targum, to the mercenary grievance and points to the fuller parallel; Henry weighs the scorn against the sound advice buried in it. Between them they show the shape of the coming war already sketched in a parable: the thistle has sent to the cedar, and the wild beast is even now abroad in Lebanon. Joash offers Amaziah, under the sting of ridicule, one last chance to draw back; and the next verse presses the same warning without the fable's veil.
19:
Joash drops the fable and speaks plainly — "thou sayest, Lo, thou hast smitten the Edomites; and thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to thine hurt?" — and the witnesses attend closely to the wording and to the diagnosis of pride within it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott shows how slightly the chronicler's phrasing differs from the older text at 2 Kings 14:10, and how the differences are matters of pointing that a copyist might make: "Lo" (hinneh) is perhaps a corruption of the word for "smiting" (hakkeh), so that the sense may be "thou hast indeed smitten"; "to boast" is literally "to get glory," a form used only here; and where Kings has "be honoured, and abide at home," the chronicler's "lifteth thee up to boast" differs by the points alone. The philology, dry in itself, lays bare the taunt's exact edge: the Edomite victory has gone to the king's head.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, give the plain drift of the counsel: thou hast smitten Edom, and thy heart has lifted thee up to boast, but abide at home — why shouldest thou meddle with misfortune, that thou shouldest fall, thou and Judah with thee? The warning is double, for the king's folly will ruin not himself only but his kingdom.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the friendly core of Joash's scornful reply — the sound advice to sit still and know when he was well off. It is precisely the counsel of Solomon that Henry had invoked at the challenge: he that goes forth hastily to strive will not know what to do in the end thereof, when his neighbour has put him to shame, at Proverbs 25:8. Amaziah is offered, by his very enemy, the wisdom his flatterers withheld: enjoy the honour thou hast won, and do not stake it on a needless war.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott traces the taunt through its fine textual variations; Keil gives its plain and ominous sense; Henry hears in it the honest advice a proud man cannot take. Between them they show the mercy hidden even in an adversary's mockery — Joash naming Amaziah's fault exactly, the swollen heart of a man who has won one battle and thinks himself invincible — and they leave the king poised on the edge of the ruin the next verse says he could not be turned from. The boast that lifts the heart up, the witnesses agree, is the surest sign that a fall is near.
20:
Amaziah will not be turned, and the chronicler lifts the veil on why — "but Amaziah would not hear; for it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom." The witnesses read the verse as the meeting of the king's obstinacy and the judgment of God. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Amaziah would not hear what the king of Israel advised, namely not to meddle to his own hurt. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the added clause as the chronicler's own, inserted to account for the king's infatuation by reference to the divine predetermination of events, and sets it beside the like theology at v.16, where the prophet had already said God had determined to destroy him, and at 2 Chronicles 24:24 and 2 Chronicles 10:15. The deliverance "into the hand," he suggests, means into the hand of Joash; and "because they sought" is better "for they had sought" — the idolatry of v.14 being the sin now answered.

Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way: Amaziah refused the warning, for it came of God to give Judah into the hand of the enemy because they had sought the gods of Edom. The obstinacy is real, and yet it serves a hidden verdict already passed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the theology with care. Amaziah's imprudence, he says, is here made the punishment of his impiety: God left him to himself, to act thus foolishly, that he and his people might be delivered into the hands of their enemies, because they had forsaken God and sought after the gods of Edom. Those who will not be persuaded to do well for their souls, Henry warns, are justly given up to their own counsels to do ill even for their outward affairs. The king is not compelled to sin against his will; he is abandoned to the pride he has chosen, and that abandonment is itself the sentence.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the refusal; Ellicott and Keil mark the chronicler's clause and its cross-references; Henry unfolds the justice of a judicial hardening. Between them they hold together two truths the verse binds in one sentence — that Amaziah would not hear, and that his not hearing was of God. The idolater who silenced the prophet is now left to the flatterers who will lead him to Beth-shemesh; his ruin is his own choice, and it is also the righteous recompense of his sin.
22:
The armies meet at Beth-shemesh, and Judah is routed — "Judah was put to the worse before Israel, and they fled every man to his tent." The witnesses, brief here, fix the defeat as the exact fulfilment of the warning Amaziah had spurned. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes only that the clause stands as in the older account at 2 Kings 14:12, and that the Syriac and Arabic versions omit the verse — a textual observation that leaves the fact untouched. Keil and Delitzsch, whose comment gathers the whole battle, set the rout in its place: Joash king of Israel went up, and the two kings saw one another in the face at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah; and there Judah was smitten before Israel and fled every man to his tent. The battle was fought, that is, on Judah's own soil, and ended in the flight of Judah's host.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names this the defeat that mortified the proud king — the plain outcome that Joash's fable had foretold and Joash's advice had tried to prevent. The thistle presumed on the cedar, and the wild beast trode it down; the boast that lifted Amaziah's heart at v.19 is answered by a scattered army fleeing to their tents. And behind the military collapse lies the verdict the previous verse pronounced: the defeat came of God, who had determined to deliver Judah into the enemy's hand because they had sought the gods of Edom. That the two kings met at Beth-shemesh, a town of Judah, only deepens the shame, for the battle Amaziah had forced upon his neighbour was fought and lost on his own ground, the war he sought abroad recoiling upon his own soil.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of their notes is itself eloquent. Ellicott secures the text; Keil narrates the meeting at Beth-shemesh and the flight; Henry reads the rout as the mortification of pride and the working-out of judgment. Between them they show how swiftly the whole proud enterprise unravelled: the king who would not be advised, marching to look his neighbour in the face, sees instead the back of his own fleeing soldiers. The war Amaziah forced upon a stronger king ends, as every witness in this chapter had said it must, not in the glory he coveted but in the shame he was warned of — his army broken, his capital exposed, and himself, as the next verse will tell, a prisoner in the hand he was determined to challenge.
23:
The defeat becomes a humiliation: Joash takes the king of Judah captive and breaches the wall of his own capital. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works through the verse's textual knots. In Amaziah's genealogy the Hebrew here names his grandfather "Jehoahaz," where several manuscripts and the parallel at 2 Kings 14:13 read "Ahaziah," with which the rest of the verse agrees — the two being the same name with its elements reversed. And the breach Joash made, from the gate of Ephraim to the "corner gate," Ellicott recovers against a Hebrew text that reads "the gate of the turning one" or "the gate that turneth"; some manuscripts and all the versions agree with Kings, and he compares the similar expression at Ezekiel 8:3 and the corner gate again at 2 Chronicles 26:9 — the whole difference, he insists, being one of vowel-points only.

Keil and Delitzsch, gathering the sequel of the battle, fix the substance: Joash took Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, brought him to Jerusalem, and broke down the wall of the city from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits — a great gap torn in the defences of the holy city by a fellow-Hebrew king. The captured king is led to his own capital only to watch its walls thrown down.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole calamity as the fruit the proud challenge bore: the defeat, the capture, and the breaching of Jerusalem's wall are the disaster Amaziah brought upon himself and his city by refusing to sit still. The four hundred cubits of ruined rampart are the visible measure of a king's folly — Judah's own defences dismantled because her king would not be warned. Henry marks too how the humiliation reaches beyond the man to the nation: the city that had done nothing suffers for the pride of the throne that led it into a needless war.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott untangles the names and the gate and the points that trouble the Hebrew; Keil fixes the capture and the four-hundred-cubit breach; Henry reads it all as the harvest of a proud man's meddling. Between them they show the depth of the reversal — the conqueror of Edom a prisoner, the city of David breached like a common town — and they leave Amaziah standing in the wreck of his own capital, the walls that should have guarded him broken open by the king he could not leave alone.
24:
The victor strips the temple and the palace and carries off hostages, and the witnesses attend to the plunder and to one detail the chronicler alone preserves. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the phrase "in the house of God with Obed-edom": from the earlier record at 1 Chronicles 26:15 we learn that to Obed-edom and his descendants was allotted the keeping of the house of Asuppim, the store or collections for the divine treasury — so the gold and silver Joash seized had lain under a hereditary Levitical guard. For the hostages Joash also took, Clarke refers the reader to the parallel at 2 Kings 14:14. John Wesley, of the same school, adds only that "Obed-edom" means the posterity of Obed-edom, to whom the custody of the sacred treasures was committed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott secures the text and weighs the addition. The verb "he took" has actually fallen out of the Hebrew here, an ancient omission already present in the Septuagint, so that the Vulgate supplies "carried back to Samaria" and the Syriac "took the silver"; the sense, however, is plain — Joash carried off all the gold and silver and vessels found in the house of God and the treasures of the king's house. And the clause "with Obed-edom," Ellicott judges, is the chronicler's own addition, in harmony with what he had recorded of the custody of the sacred treasures at 1 Chronicles 26:15, but probably drawn from an ancient document, Obed-edom being the name of a Levitical clan. It is the kind of circumstantial detail that marks the chronicler's independent sources.

Brief as the notices are, the witnesses let the weight of the loss show. This is no foreign invader but a brother-king rifling the house of God — the treasures of the temple and the palace alike borne away to Samaria, and hostages taken to secure the peace. The very treasury guarded by Obed-edom's line since David's day is emptied by an Israelite hand, and the humiliation Amaziah began with a proud challenge ends with the sanctuary itself plundered.

The witnesses do not divide. Clarke and Wesley fix the Levitical custody of the treasures Joash seized; Ellicott mends the dropped verb and traces the chronicler's added detail to an old record. Between them they show the full cost of the king's folly reaching even into the temple: the gold that Judah's piety had gathered under a faithful guard is carried north as a spoil, and the reign that had begun by honouring the law of God closes its war by seeing the house of God stripped bare.
25:
A single chronological line closes the war and opens the reign's long anticlimax — Amaziah outlived his conqueror Joash of Israel by fifteen years. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse is identical with the older record at 2 Kings 14:17, the chronicler simply taking over the synchronism that fixes Amaziah's survival against the death of the northern king. The bare arithmetic carries a quiet irony: the man who forced the war and lost it lived on a decade and a half after the rival who had beaten him, captured him, and stripped his capital — a survival that was no triumph but a slow decline.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the character of those fifteen years. Amaziah, he observes, became very unpopular after losing the battle with Israel, the consequences being the dismantling of Jerusalem's wall and the seizure of the royal and sacred treasures; it is likely, Clarke judges, that the last fifteen years of his reign were greatly embittered, the defeated king lingering under the resentment of subjects who could not forgive the humiliation he had brought on them. The long survival, in other words, was fifteen years of diminished and grudging rule.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same span as the slow gathering of the storm that would kill him. From the time that Amaziah departed from the LORD, Henry says, the hearts of his subjects departed from him, and they began to form their design against him in Jerusalem; it was probably his rash war against Israel, even more than his idolatry, that exasperated them. The fifteen years are thus the interval in which a king already defeated abroad became hated at home — the reprieve was not a mercy the nation gave him but a delay before the conspiracy the next verses record.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the synchronism and its parallel in Kings; Clarke reads the fifteen years as embittered and unpopular; Henry watches the subjects' loyalty drain away through them. Between them they turn a dry chronological note into the hinge of the reign's last act. Amaziah's survival of Joash proves nothing to his credit; it merely lengthens the shadow. The proud king who would look his neighbour in the face lived on to look his own people in the face and find their hearts turned from him — fifteen years of a life that had already, in every way that mattered, been defeated.
26:
The formal close of the reign begins with the customary appeal to the royal annals, and the witnesses read the standing formula with an eye to its sources and its careful phrasing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last, are referred to "the book of the kings of Judah and Israel" — the composite chronicle of the divided monarchy from which the sacred writer so often draws, and on which they had commented in their Introduction. The single reign is signed off, that is, with a pointer to the fuller record that lay behind the compiler's own.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on the phrase "first and last" and gives it the Targum's fine moral reading: the first acts, when Amaziah walked in the fear of the LORD, and the last, when he departed from the right way before the LORD. The formula, on this reading, is not a bare bibliographical note but a quiet summary of the whole divided life — a reign of two halves, the good beginning and the bad end that the opening verses had foretold.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his usual textual care to the wording. "First and last" he renders "the former and the latter," the chronicler's habitual formula; but the following clause is faulty in the Hebrew, for "Behold, are they not written" blends two distinct phrases — the chronicler's customary "Behold, they are written," as at other closing-notices, with the "are they not written" that belongs rather to the book of Kings. Some manuscripts and the Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic read the plain "Behold, they are written"; and Ellicott suggests the odd word may be a corruption, so that the reading of Kings should be followed. It is the sort of small seam where the compiler's transcribing hand shows through.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil fixes the source and its title; Clarke draws from "first and last" the Targum's picture of a reign of two moral halves; Ellicott secures the phrasing and marks the blended formula. Between them they show the chronicler doing what he does at every reign's end — deferring the political detail to the older annals while he presses his own theological point. And the point is written into the very formula: Amaziah's story divides, "first and last," into a season when he feared the LORD and a season when he forsook him, and it is that division, not the annals of his deeds, that the sacred writer most wants remembered.
27:
The reign ends as the prophet had said it would, in conspiracy and flight and a violent death. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch relate the sequel: from the time that Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem; he fled to Lachish, but they sent after him and slew him there. They note too the textual oddity that the following verse calls his burial-place "the city of Judah," where everywhere else, and in all the ancient versions, it is "the city of David" — an orthographical slip, they judge, for "David," occasioned by the "Judah" that stands beside it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the opening clause as the theological heart of the notice. "Now after the time that Amaziah did turn away from following the LORD" is added by the chronicler, he says, not so much to fix a date as to assert the real connection between the king's defection from Jehovah and the calamities that overtook him; virtually the compiler is calling attention to the fulfilment of the prophet's word at v.16, that God had determined to destroy him. The conspiracy is not mere palace politics but the working-out of a sentence pronounced long before.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the human causes. Amaziah became deeply unpopular after losing the battle, with the dismantling of Jerusalem and the seizure of the royal treasures; finding the capital no place of safety, he fled to Lachish, but his murderers pursued him thither. He who forsook the LORD, Clarke reflects, was forsaken by every friend, perished in his gainsaying, and came to an untimely end. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same providence: from the time Amaziah departed from the LORD the hearts of his subjects departed from him; the conspiracy grew until he thought fit to quit his royal city, but they sent after him and slew him — and however unrighteous the conspirators, God was righteous in it.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil narrates the flight and death and mends the "city of Judah"; Ellicott binds the whole catastrophe to the king's apostasy and the prophet's word; Clarke and Henry trace the loss of every friend and the departing of every heart. Between them they close the reign exactly where its ruin began — at the turning away from the LORD in v.14. The idolater who silenced his reprover is hunted down by his own people; the sentence the prophet spoke and the king would not hear is executed at Lachish; and the chronicler will have the reader see, in the assassin's knife, the long arm of a judgment the king himself had invited.
28:
The body is brought home for burial, and the chapter closes on a quiet death-notice whose only difficulty is a single misspelled word. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the plain fact: they brought Amaziah upon horses and buried him with his fathers in the city — the slain king carried back to Jerusalem for interment among the kings of Judah. But they pause, as at the previous verse, over the reading "the city of Judah," which is surprising, since everywhere else the royal burial-place is named "the city of David," and even here all the ancient versions have "city of David"; "Judah," they conclude, must be an orthographical error for "David," occasioned by the immediately following word.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees at both points. "Upon horses" he refers to the parallel notice at 2 Kings 14:20, where the same detail of the corpse borne on horseback is given; and "in the city of Judah" he calls a transcriber's mistake for "city of David," as it stands in Kings, in all the old versions, and in some Hebrew manuscripts. The point on which both witnesses converge is that the text as it stands says a little less than the writer meant, and the parallel and the versions restore it.

Brief as the notice is, its placement gives it weight. The proud king who forced a war, lost it, and was hunted to his death at Lachish is nonetheless brought back in something like honour — carried on horses to the capital and laid with his fathers, so that the outward forms of a royal burial are not denied him. Yet the honour is bare and formal, granted to a man his people had conspired against and killed; and the chapter that opened with a king "established" on his throne and doing right in the sight of the LORD ends with his body carried home to a grave he reached by way of apostasy, defeat, and assassination.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the burial, mend the misspelled name against the parallel and the versions, and leave the reign to close on its melancholy note. Between them they set down the last of Amaziah — buried, like better kings, with his fathers in the city of David, but remembered by the chronicler not for the good beginning that gave him the throne so much as for the divided heart that lost it. The horses that bear him home carry the ruin of a reign that a whole heart toward God might have spared.
